record.title: SIFT uses pairwise judging and disaggregated search to improve recursive coding-agent benchmarks
record.summary: A Sep 17, 2026 arXiv preprint introduces SIFT, which uses pairwise LLM judgments and a regularized Bradley–Terry ranking signal to steer a disaggregated search over coding-agent modifications, reserving more expensive task evaluations for selected candidates. The authors report Polyglot gains over named recursive-search baselines and a TerminalBench result where judge-ranked selection outperforms selection by search-subset score across three repeated full evaluations. These are author-reported results from one preprint. A resource table and adjacent prose disagree substantially on the o3-mini/GPT-5.4 run's steps, cost and CPU time, so the paper's efficiency comparison is not resolved here.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: SIFT uses pairwise LLM judgments of candidate code patches, aggregates wins and losses with a regularized Bradley–Terry model, and uses those scores for rank-based parent sampling in a disaggregated search pipeline; expensive task evaluations are reserved for selected nodes.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the authors' Polyglot-225 experiments, SIFT with Qwen3-Coder-30B and a Qwen3-Coder-480B judge reaches 31.1%, compared with 30.5% for HGM in the reported comparison. With o3-mini and a GPT-5.4 judge, SIFT reaches 35.1%, compared with 30.7% for DGM, which the paper says used 80 search nodes while the SIFT run used 30 expansion steps.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On TerminalBench 2.1, the authors report three repeated full evaluations averaging 36.7% for the agent selected by judge rank and 28.1% for the agent selected by search-score rank, after search used a sampled 50-task subset.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The v1 paper's resource accounting is internally inconsistent for the o3-mini/GPT-5.4 SIFT result: Table 3 lists 20 expansion steps, $86.8 API cost, 59 CPU hours and 2.1 hours wall time, while adjacent prose describes 30 steps, $150 in credits, 42 CPU hours and under five hours. This review does not reconcile the figures.

evidence_gaps.description: The paper's Table 3 and adjacent prose disagree on steps, API credits and CPU hours for the o3-mini/GPT-5.4 SIFT run.
No independent reproduction of the Polyglot or TerminalBench results was located or performed.
No implementation repository link appears in the arXiv record inspected for v1.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported results hold, pairwise patch judging that reduces expensive benchmark evaluations could change how teams allocate compute in recursive coding-agent search. A 5 reflects a notable but currently single-paper advance in a specialist frontier; the results are author-reported and a material run-cost discrepancy remains unresolved.
limitations: All performance results are author-reported in a single arXiv preprint; no independent reproduction was performed.
The o3-mini/GPT-5.4 resource totals and expansion-step count conflict between Table 3 and adjacent prose; resource efficiency cannot be inferred from that row without clarification.
The reported comparisons use specific coding, expansion and judge models; transfer to other models, patch distributions and agent harnesses is not established generally.
TerminalBench search uses a 50-task subset before repeated full evaluations; selected-agent outcomes do not establish that judge ranking is reliable across task distributions.
No public source-code link was listed on the arXiv record during this review, and no execution was attempted.
brief.summary: A Sep 17, 2026 arXiv preprint introduces SIFT, which uses pairwise LLM judgments and a regularized Bradley–Terry ranking signal to steer a disaggregated search over coding-agent modifications, reserving more expensive task evaluations for selected candidates. The authors report Polyglot gains over named recursive-search baselines and a TerminalBench result where judge-ranked selection outperforms selection by search-subset score across three repeated full evaluations. These are author-reported results from one preprint. A resource table and adjacent prose disagree substantially on the o3-mini/GPT-5.4 run's steps, cost and CPU time, so the paper's efficiency comparison is not resolved here.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report Polyglot-225 gains in Qwen3-Coder-30B and o3-mini configurations and a TerminalBench 2.1 selection result. Results are limited to the paper's evaluated harnesses and benchmarks.
technical.compute_or_cost: The authors report CPU-hour, wall-clock and API-cost savings, but Table 3's o3-mini/GPT-5.4 row (20 steps, $86.8, 59 CPU hours, 2.1 hours) conflicts with adjacent prose (30 steps, $150, 42 CPU hours, under five hours). Do not use that row as a reconciled cost estimate.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible arXiv v1 documents the method, experiment descriptions, tables and an internal inconsistency in one run's resource accounting. No independent code execution or reproduction was performed.
technical.mechanism: An LLM judge compares candidate patches pairwise against selected incumbents. A regularized Bradley–Terry fit aggregates the win-loss results; ranks guide parent sampling and an asynchronous evaluation queue in a disaggregated tree search. Full benchmark execution remains the selection signal for promising nodes.
technical.regime: arXiv:2609.19526v1, submitted Sep 17, 2026. Polyglot-225 includes Qwen3-Coder-30B and o3-mini agent configurations with different judge models. TerminalBench search uses a sampled 50-task subset and reports repeated full evaluation over 89 tasks. Results are author-reported.
technical.reproducibility: The full v1 HTML is available on arXiv. No code link is listed on the arXiv record and no independent reproduction was located or performed in this review. The arXiv record lists only v1; the exact resource discrepancy remains unresolved.
technical.strongest_baseline: For Qwen3-Coder-30B, the paper reports 31.1% for SIFT versus 30.5% for HGM. For o3-mini with GPT-5.4 judge it reports 35.1% versus 30.7% for DGM, but the paper compares 30 SIFT expansion steps with 80 DGM search nodes. On TerminalBench the judge-ranked candidate's repeated evaluation mean exceeds the candidate chosen by search-subset accuracy; this is a selector comparison, not a matched generalization claim.

brief.title: SIFT uses pairwise judging and disaggregated search to improve recursive coding-agent benchmarks
brief.why_it_matters: If independently reproduced with reconciled accounting, cheap pairwise judging could help recursive coding-agent research spend fewer benchmark runs on weak candidate modifications. The current evidence is one author-run preprint; it does not establish a general compute advantage, and its reported resource figures conflict for a key run.
